clues.title: Bollard: Bollard
text: Standard Spanish bollards have a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots on the back, though the back can sometimes be blank. They are typically hollow.

clues.title: Sign: No hunting sign
text: In rural areas of Spain, you will often find no hunting signs. There are two versions, both unique to Spain. One is a simple white sign with text starting with "coto" and ending in "caza." The other has a diagonally divided black and white background.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Aranese
text: Aranese is a language spoken only by about 2,800 people in Val d'Aran (Catalonia region of Spain west of Andorra on French border), most notably the town of Vielha. It looks very similar to Catalan and the street names are the easiest way of identifying it. Although uncommon recognizing it could give you an easy high scoring guess.
**carrèr** - (carrer in Catalan, look for the accent on the "e")
**avenguda** - (avinguda in Catalan)
**passeg** - (passeig in Catalan)
Other clues that may help you guess Val d'Aran is that it is a mountainous region with many rock buildings similar to Andorra.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Galician
text: Galician is a romance language spoken in Spain in the area north of portugal. Unsurprisingly given it's proximity it is closely related to portuguese. In addition to the tips below the most helpful tip is to look for town names that have "A(s)" or "O(s)" in front of them ( “A Pena”, “O Burgo”, “As Cruces”). This is ALMOST unique to the galician area of Spain to see this.
uses ñ like spanish
Doesn't use ç
uses "nh" diagraph like portuguese but words end in -ción like spanish
heavier usage of the letter "x"

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Basque Country Spain
text: Road signs in the Basque Country and Navarre often have these distinctive bilingual sub-signs with a thick black border. Generally you will find Basque on top in the Basque Country, while it is more common to find Spanish on top in Navarre.
Streets in Basque-speaking areas are sometimes called “kalea”. However, Spanish “calle” is also still common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Street sign: Catalan Valencian Community
text: The Valencian community in Spain also uses catalan but to a lesser extent than Catalonia. You will see more bilingual and spanish only signs but most street signs will still use the word "carrer".

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Spanish General Tips
text: Here are some general tips to recognize Spanish:
Ñ is ALMOST unique to Spnaish (exception = Galician)
¿ ¡ inverted question and exclamation marks are common
and = "y"
Some words frequently used: de, el, del, los, la(s), uno(s), una(s)
Word endings: -o, -a, -ción, -miento, -dad
double l "ll" more common than other romance languages (Catalan exception)

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Spanish Helpful Words
text: Here are a few words in Spanish that can either help you identify the language quickly, be helpful in region guessing, or just help learn the general feel of the language:
**centro ciudad** - city center
**estación** - station
**iglesia** - church
**excepto** - except
**aparcamiento** - parking
**parador** - stop
**salida** - exit
**parque** - park
**todas direcciones** - all directions
**venta** - sale
**se vende** - for sale
**se alquila** - for rent

clues.title: Street in Spanish
text: **"Calle"** is the word for street in Spanish. Here are some other related words:
**pasaje** - passage/alleyway
**avenida** - avenue
**camino** - way/path
**carretera** - highway

NOTE: The only other European country with 8 stripes is Andorra.

clues.title: Route marker: Road Markers
text: Spain has distinct road markers, easy to recognize being **usually square** and having **colourful borders**. The code on top is the **number of the road**.
**NOTE:**: The letter codes before the road number on these markers are often an important region-specific clue, check **plonkit** for all the code regions.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Ladder poles
text: In Spain, these concrete **ladder** poles can be found amongst other types. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.
**NOTE:** France can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

**NOTE:** Very close to Andorra, you can find a slightly different bollard, which is also used in Andorra itself.

clues.title: Landscape: Aragon Dryness
text: Very arid looking and mostly flat areas are common in central and south Aragón. The soil is very white and rocky in the northern part. Red soil is more common in Teruel.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Castilla La Mancha
text: Castilla la Mancha can have completely flat landscapes. Half of Spain’s wine is produced in this region, so vineyards are fairly common. In the western provinces of Ciudad Real and Toledo, it is very common to see olive tree plantations, generally in flatter ground than those found in Andalusia.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Navarra Semi Desert
text: Starting in Navarra and cutting across the middle of Aragón, there is a strip of semi-desert landscape on both sides of the Ebro river basin. Light sandy soil and small shrubs growing on small hills are common in this area.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Lanzarote Volcanic Rock
text: In some parts of the island of Lanzarote on the Canary Islands, a very dark, exposed volcanic soil can be seen. In places, this landscape superficially resembles the surface of the moon.
NOTE: The other Canary Islands can sometimes have similar landscapes as well, but it is by far the most common on Lanzarote.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Fuerteventura
text: The island of Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands is characterised by a very arid landscape with little to no vegetation. Orange soil is very common, and within the Canary Islands archipelago essentially unique to this island.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: CastillaYLeon
text: The centre of Castilla y León features a mostly flat agricultural landscape, with only slight changes in elevation. Most of the fields will have cereal crops like wheat and barley, and it is fairly common to find sunflower plantations.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Formentera
text: The small island of Formentera frequently features low coastal shrubs. It is common to be able to see the mountains of Ibiza from Formentera’s north coast.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Pyrenees
text: The Pyrenees is a large mountain range on the border between Spain and France. Its mountains are some of the highest in all of Spain. It can be recognized by its light grey rock and abundance of pine trees. Local architecture features many rock walls.
NOTE: Andorra and the Spanish part of the Pyrenees look very similar in terms of landscape and architecture. And consider that the exclave of Llívia is part of Spain.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Northeast
text: The landscape in the far north is much more green and lush than the rest of Spain. The landscape is generally quite hilly. Hedges and green meadows are common. In some places, this region’s landscape bears a vague resemblance to Ireland, France and the UK.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Ebro Delta
text: The Ebro delta (Deltebre in catalan) features an extremely flat landscape, where rice fields and water canals are very common. There are significant mountains to the South, West, and North, and some of them can be seen from almost every location in the delta.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Sierra Nevada National Park
text: The mountain range of Sierra Nevada features snowy peaks through the months of November and May. Sierra Nevada is the only mountain range in south Spain with snow during most of the year.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Rural Dashed Outlines
text: Rural roads sometimes have dashed outer lines.
This can help tell Spain apart from Portugal and Italy, where such road lines are (almost) non-existent.
**The reverse is not true:**
Like Italy and Portugal, many Spanish roads do have solid outer lines.

As the name suggests, French poletops are also very common in France.

clues.title: Architecture: Galicia - Big Concrete Blocks
text: Many houses in Galicia are built with big concrete blocks, sometimes textured to resemble natural stone.
Plain concrete blocks are also an extremely common material for walls and miscellaneous buildings like garages.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Northwest - Slate Roofs
text: There is a large part of north-west Spain where you will find almost exclusively slate roofs (recognisable by their almost black colour).
This type of roofing can be seen sparingly all the way to the west coast of Galicia, but ends rather abruptly on the east.
Slate roofs can also be found in the Pyrenees near Andorra, and in the mountain ranges north east of Madrid.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Galicia - Cabazos
text: In Galicia, these unique granaries called “horreos gallegos”, or “cabazos”, are very common.
Note that they can be made from various materials, but the shape remains the same.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Asturias - Square Hórreos
text: In Asturias, “hórreos” are bigger, generally with a square design, and are built above four pillars, with or without walls.
You will sometimes find a rectangular variation, usually built on top of six or eight pillars called “panera”.
If you find an “horreo” with a slate roof, you will be in western Asturias.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Basque - White Houses
text: Large white houses with wooden frames are common in the Basque Country, the Basque part of Navarra, and Cantabria.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Catalonia & Aragón - Masias
text: Traditional farm houses called “masías” are common in Catalonia, eastern Aragón and parts of the Valencian Community.
They are usually made of stone and stand isolated or as part of a small complex.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Balearic - Full White Houses
text: The stereotypical Balearic house is painted completely white.
You can find flat roofs, but tiled roofs with a small incline are the most common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Centre & South - White Towns
text: Within the centre and south of Spain, towns made completely out of white painted houses are very common in Andalucía and Extremadura.
You can still see a fair amount of white painted houses in Castilla la Mancha but streets where every house is white will not be common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Spain
text: Area codes in Spain are very useful, as you only need two digits to get a very accurate guess. Every landline number starts with “9”, followed by the regional numbers.
Mobile numbers start with “6”, and are not relevant in region guessing.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Aragón Bollard
text: In Aragón, it is common to see this bollard design on regional roads.
It has a simple design, consisting of a short flat rectangular white stick with a grey reflector on both sides.
**NOTE:** There are similar bollards in other regions, but they appear much less frequently than in Aragón.

clues.title: Pole: ladder pole
text: In Spain, you can find a variety of electricity poles and pole tops. In small towns and sparsely populated rural areas concrete ladder poles and wooden poles are the most common.
“Ladder” poles have indents that resemble a ladder, hence the name.

clues.title: Pole: french style
text: “French style” poletops are common in Spain. They are shaped like an upside down triangle, with a horizontal top bar that is curved slightly upwards. They are usually found on top of tall ladder poles or medium sized steel poles.
NOTE: As the name suggests, French poletops are also very common in France.

clues.title: Pole: steel mesh rectangular
text: Poles with a steel mesh structure making rectangular shapes instead of the typical triangles can be found in the southern half of Spain, and are particularly common in Murcia and southern Alicante.

clues.title: Language: Catalan language - carrer
text: If you're in Spain and see a street sign with "Carrer" instead of "Calle", you're likely in a Catalan -speaking region, such as Catalonia, Valencia, or the Balearic Islands.
Andorra also uses Catalan as its official language.

clues.title: Language: Catalan
text: Catalan is a Romance language closely related to Spanish and French. In Spain, it is spoken in Catalonia, the Valencian Community, and the Balearic Islands. In Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, it is (much) more common than Spanish on signage. The Valencian Community is more bilingual.
The Catalan word for street is **carrer**. This is unlike Spainsh where it is **calle**.

If you are unfamiliar with Romance languages, it can otherwise be hard to distinguish between Catalan and Spanish. If you see **i** instead of **y** (“and” in English), it is Catalan. In addition, more Catalan words end with consonants.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Basque
text: Basque is a language isolate spoken in adjacent parts of northern Spain and southwestern France. It has a unique look, not resembling any other language, commonly including the letters **K, X** and **Z**. In Spain, you will find a mix of Spanish and Basque signs (often bilingual) in the Basque Country and northern Navarre.
Streets in Basque-speaking areas of Spain are sometimes called **kalea** (in France **karrika** instead). However, Spanish **calle** is also still common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Spanish
text: Spanish is a Romance language closely related to Portuguese. Spanish and Portuguese can look very similar. Some key differences between the two:
**Ñ** is unique to Spanish.
**Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, Ê** and **lh** are unique to Portuguese (**Ç** is also present in Catalan).
Portuguese uses the **-ao** word ending, and **-nh-** instead of **ñ**.
Spanish uses **de** and **del**, while these are often contracted to **da**, **do**, **das** and **dos** in Portuguese.
The Spanish word for street is **calle**.
